title: The small things
hookLine: the Buddha refrains from even small unkindness, like idle talk and shows
carry: the ground the summit stands on

cards: Board games on eight-row and ten-row boards. Games played on imaginary boards in the air. Dice.
Toy plows and toy windmills. Guessing what a friend is thinking. Elephant fights, ballad singers, acrobats.
This is a real list, from the first long discourse, a snapshot of what people did for fun long ago. It's there because the Buddha is describing what he doesn't do.
These little things, he says, are what an ordinary person praises him for.

teach.b: When an ordinary person praises me, he tells the monks, it's for small matters, mere moral conduct. Then he lists them.

teach.h: NO STICK, NO SWORD, NO TALE-BEARING
teach.b: He's put down the stick and the sword. He's gentle and kind, compassionate toward all living beings. He takes only what's given.
He speaks the truth; he's reliable. He doesn't carry tales from one group to another to split them apart; he brings together those who are divided, and enjoys harmony. His speech isn't harsh.
It's pleasant to the ear, it goes to the heart. He doesn't waste words, and speaks at the right time, about what's true and useful. Then the finer points.
He doesn't damage seeds or plants.

teach.h: NO SHOWS, NO GAMES, NO LOW TALK
teach.b: He doesn't go to shows: dancing, singing, music, those elephant fights. He doesn't play the games. He doesn't trade in false weights and measures.
He doesn't pass the day in what the text calls low talk: kings and robbers, food and clothes, gossip at the well. The Pali word for all this is sila: moral conduct, virtue. And here's the twist.

teach.h: SMALL, BUT THE GROUND OF IT ALL
teach.b: The Buddha calls it small. The real teaching is deeper, and the rest of the discourse goes there.
But he practices every one of the small things anyway. They aren't the summit. They're the ground the summit stands on.

how: Lay Buddhists keep five precepts, and in Theravada communities some take eight on observance days, which add refraining from entertainments, adornment and luxurious beds: a lay echo of the conduct listed in DN 1.

o: a rule that only monks must keep
a vow to keep total silence

games.q: the small things: tap the pairs.
p: not carried from group to group
kings, robbers, gossip at the well

s: the Buddha says ordinary people praise him for his deepest teaching
he says they praise him for small matters of moral conduct.
the list includes board games and elephant fights
a real snapshot of ancient entertainments the Buddha didn't take part in.
because the Buddha calls these things small, he skips them
he practices every one; they're the ground the deeper teaching stands on.

games.q: two groups of friends have fallen out, and you've heard what each says about the other. according to DN 1's list, what does the Buddha do in this spot?
o: brings divided people together and enjoys harmony.
repeats each side's words to the other.
games.why: he doesn't carry tales from one group to another to split them; he brings together those who are divided.

practice: Go through the list slowly, gentle speech, no carrying tales, speaking at the right time, not wasting words, taking only what's given, and let the one closest to your actual life light up.
Picture the moment it usually comes, see yourself meeting it with a little more care, then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Sila. Moral conduct, virtue, in its smallest forms: kind speech, no gossip, careful hands. Small, and still practiced.

orig.note: Pali sila (Sanskrit shila): moral conduct, virtue, the ground of practice.

carryVoice: Your line: the ground the summit stands on. He called it small, and kept every piece. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 1, Brahmajala Sutta, the sections on moral conduct
